newsitem.title: UK: LME copper recovers from lows by close.
newsitem.headline: LME copper recovers from lows by close.

text.p: Base metals snapped back from their lows by Friday's London Metal Exchange (LME) close as recent market leader copper again rallied and attacked resistance above $1,950, traders said.
Late flurries of borrowing of tight nearby spreads prompted short covering which lifted prices to unchanged levels from Thursday at $1,958, against a low of $1,919.
The cash to three months backwardation flared to around $40 from $32 earlier. Supporting the late snap was the markets ability to hold trendline support near $1,920.
Traders suggested a move below this key chart level could have sparked a retracement to $1,900.
But despite another LME stocks fall of 8,000 tonnes benchmark three months delivery copper failed to make any significant upside inroads.
"Overall the market continues to range trade roughly between $1,900 and $2,000...its been hit by profit-taking on any upside probes," one LME floor trader commented.
Copper's near-term direction now hinges on LME warehouse stocks which currently stand at six-year lows of 123,700 tonnes.
Some solace was derived from the continuing stock declines, with the overall picture bolstered by a modest delivery of 1,100 tonnes into Singapore.
Recently there has been concern of much bigger arrivals in Singapore, which could suggest the recent Chinese liftings are not for consumption.
Also upside market caution was aired by several traders, believing that the run of stock drawdowns was reaching its end.
Another fall in zinc stocks aided an earlier rally to 5-1/2 month highs of $1,075. The move was also bolstered by recent investment fund buying and uptrending charts.
Final three months business was near to this level at $1,073.50 versus $1,066.
Traders said zinc has the potential to climb further towards $1,100, although any weakening in copper prices could dent upside sentiment.
Nickel retreated after earlier relinquishing the $7,300 level under trade selling. A 90-tonne stock increase also helped to knock upside sentiment.
Physical traders said supplies of Russian nickel and stainless steel scrap are still plentiful in Western Europe.
Although orders books have picked up slightly, the stock overhang could delay a strong pick up in the physical market until well into 1997, they added.
It was last at $7,190, against $7,330.
Aluminium slipped back after a hefty 10,250-tonne stock increase. Traders said a challenge of $1,400 is seen near-term after prices lost upside momentum around $1,450.
Aluminium was last at $1,425, down $13.
Lead was quiet throughout and was last at $751, a loss of $1, while tin settled at $5,975, versus $5,985.
Alloy was quoted at $1,270/75, down from $1,290.
